lessons.title: Course Requirements
lessons.content:
To fully benefit from the "Mastering the Dividend Capture Strategy with Options" course, students must meet the following requirements:

  1. Familiarity with Options Basics:

    • Level 1: Long Call
      • Understanding the fundamentals of buying call options, including when and why to use this strategy.
    • Level 2: Short Call
      • Knowledge of selling call options, including potential risks and rewards.
    • Level 3: Long Put
      • Grasping the basics of buying put options to profit from declining stock prices.
    • Level 4: Short Put
      • Understanding the strategy of selling put options and the associated obligations.
    • Level 5: Theta and Time Decay
      • Comprehensive understanding of how time decay affects options pricing.
    • Level 6: Vega and Volatility
      • Knowledge of implied volatility and its impact on options pricing.
    • Level 7: Delta Effect
      • Understanding how delta measures an option's sensitivity to changes in the price of the underlying asset.
    • Level 8: Combined Examination
      • Ability to combine all the above concepts and apply them in case scenarios for a thorough understanding.

  2. Familiarity with Advanced Options Strategies:

    • Back Spread
      • Understanding the mechanics and applications of back spread strategies.
    • Bear Put Spread
      • Knowledge of constructing and using bear put spreads to profit from declining markets.
    • Bull Call Spread
      • Grasping the strategy of bull call spreads to profit from rising markets.
    • Butterfly
      • Understanding the butterfly spread strategy for neutral market outlooks.
    • Calendar
      • Knowledge of calendar spreads and their use in trading.
    • Covered Call
      • Understanding the covered call strategy to generate income from owned stocks.
    • Short Straddle
      • Grasping the short straddle strategy and its implications.
    • Short Strangle
      • Understanding the short strangle strategy for range-bound markets.
    • Additional Strategies
      • Familiarity with other advanced strategies taught in Options America.

This foundational knowledge is essential for understanding and applying the dividend capture strategies with options effectively. We teach these concepts in detail, and you can access these lessons and more by subscribing to Options America. If you need to review these concepts, we recommend subscribing and going through the relevant courses provided by Options America before starting this course.

lessons.title: Important Risk Disclaimer for Options Trading
lessons.content:
Trading options involves significant risk and is not suitable for every investor. The "Mastering the Dividend Capture Strategy with Options" course, provided by Options America, is designed for educational purposes only. The strategies and examples discussed are meant to provide insights and a foundational understanding of options trading; however, they do not guarantee profit or prevent losses.

  1. Market Risk:

    • Options trading is highly speculative and can result in substantial losses. Market conditions can change rapidly, and the value of options can fluctuate significantly, potentially leading to a loss of your entire investment.

  2. Leverage Risk:

    • Options leverage can amplify gains but also magnifies losses. Using leverage in your trading can result in larger losses than the initial investment.

  3. Liquidity Risk:

    • Some options may have limited liquidity, making it difficult to enter or exit positions at favorable prices. This can impact your ability to manage risk effectively.

  4. Volatility Risk:

    • Options prices are influenced by changes in volatility. Unexpected changes in volatility can impact the profitability of your positions and lead to significant losses.

  5. Time Decay:

    • The value of options erodes over time due to time decay (Theta). Understanding the impact of time decay is crucial, as it can affect the profitability of options positions.

  6. Assignment Risk:

    • Short options positions may be assigned at any time before expiration, regardless of the in-the-money status. This can result in unexpected obligations and potential losses.

  7. Knowledge and Experience:

    • Successful options trading requires a comprehensive understanding of the market, strategies, and risks involved. It is essential to continuously educate yourself and stay updated on market conditions.

  8. No Guarantee of Profit:

    • The educational content provided in this course is not a guarantee of future performance or profitability. Past performance of strategies discussed does not predict or guarantee future results.

  9. Professional Advice:

    • The information provided in this course should not be considered as financial or investment advice. Consult with a professional financial advisor to determine the appropriateness of these strategies in relation to your individual financial situation and risk tolerance.

Disclaimer: Options America, its instructors, and affiliates are not responsible for any losses incurred as a result of applying the strategies discussed in this course. By participating in this course, you acknowledge and accept the inherent risks associated with options trading.

Educational Purpose: This course is intended for educational purposes only. It aims to provide insights into the dividend capture strategy with options and is not an endorsement or recommendation for any specific trading strategy or investment.

By enrolling in this course, you agree to understand and accept the risks associated with options trading. Always perform your own due diligence and consult with a professional advisor before making any trading decisions.

lessons.title: What will we learn in Module 2
Analyzing IBM Stock and Understanding Profit and Loss
Analyzing a Sold Call Option on IBM
Analyzing Combined Stock and Sold Call Option
Covered Call Strategy Upside Downside Analysis
Summary of Dividend Capture Strategy with Covered Calls
lessons.content:
This module provides a comprehensive overview of the dividend capture strategy using covered calls. It begins by defining the strategy, which involves buying a stock before its ex-dividend date and selling it shortly after to capture the dividend payment. This approach aims to enhance returns by combining stock ownership with options strategies.

Key dates in the dividend capture process are crucial. These include the declaration date when the company announces the dividend, the ex-dividend date which is the cutoff for being eligible for the dividend, the record date when the company checks its records, and the payment date when the dividend is paid out.

The module then delves into analyzing stocks with options. Using IBM as an example, it explains the profit/loss dynamics of buying 100 shares and the impact of selling a call option. Combining these positions creates a bullish stance with positive delta, offering profit from slow increases in the underlying asset and providing limited profit potential while reducing the breakeven point for downside protection.

The dividend capture strategy with covered calls enhances returns by capturing both dividends and premiums from selling call options. This approach increases profit potential on the upside and provides further downside protection by reducing the breakeven point through dividend payments.

Practical examples illustrate how holding 100 shares of IBM and incorporating options can impact overall profit and breakeven points. The importance of selecting dividend-paying stocks, optimal timing for trades, and managing risks are emphasized to ensure a successful application of the strategy.

lessons.title: Introduction to Protective Puts and Dividend Capture
Analyzing Stock Preformance and Risk Management
Combining Stock with Protective Puts for Dividend Capture
Understanding Timing of Protective Puts with Ex-Dividend Dates
lessons.content:
Understanding Timing of Protective Puts with Ex-Dividend Dates

Combining Stocks and Protective Puts Using protective puts with stocks is a strategy that involves purchasing a put option to safeguard against potential losses in the stock. This strategy ensures that the maximum loss is limited to the cost of the put option, making it an effective risk management tool.

Capturing Dividends One of the key benefits of this strategy is the ability to capture dividends. By timing the purchase of the stock and the put option before the ex-dividend date, investors can secure the dividend payout while being protected against significant declines in the stock price.

Calculating Potential Losses and Gains When incorporating protective puts, it is essential to calculate the potential losses and gains accurately. The cost of the put option should be factored in, along with the dividend payout. This combined approach reduces the net loss and provides a clear picture of the overall risk and reward.

Reducing the Breakeven Point The dividend received can effectively reduce the breakeven point of the investment. This reduction means the stock does not need to increase as much to reach profitability, providing a buffer against minor price fluctuations.

Investment Strategy and Risk Management This strategy allows for a diversified investment approach. By spreading investments across multiple stocks, each protected with a put option, the overall portfolio risk is managed more effectively. This method ensures that even in the event of a market downturn, losses are minimized.

Conclusion Timing protective puts with ex-dividend dates combines the benefits of dividend capture with risk management. This strategy leverages options to enhance investment returns while providing a safety net against potential losses. It is a powerful approach for investors looking to maximize their returns and protect their portfolios.

lessons.title: Overview of Synthetic Long Position for Dividend Capture
Synthetic Long Position for IBM Dividend Capture
Do You Need to Exercise Your Call Options to Capture Dividends?
Synthetic Options for Dividend Capture
lessons.content:
In this module, we explore the concept of creating synthetic long positions using options to effectively capture dividends. This strategy allows traders to replicate the payoff of holding a long stock position without actually owning the stock, thus managing risk and capital more efficiently.

Key Points:

  1. Introduction to Synthetic Long Positions:

    • A synthetic long position is created by buying a call option and selling a put option with the same strike price and expiration date. This setup mimics the payoff of holding the underlying stock.

  2. Benefits of Synthetic Long Positions:

    • Capital Efficiency: Significantly reduces the capital required compared to buying the stock outright.
    • Risk Management: Limits potential losses compared to holding the stock directly.
    • Dividend Capture: Allows traders to benefit from the stock's price movement and capture the dividend as if they held the stock.

  3. Setting Up the Synthetic Long Position:

    • Identify the Ex-Dividend Date: Determine the ex-dividend date of the stock to ensure eligibility for the dividend.
    • Buy a Call Option: Choose a call option with a strike price close to the current stock price and an expiration date after the ex-dividend date.
    • Sell a Put Option: Select a put option with the same strike price and expiration date as the call option.

  4. Real-World Example: IBM:

    • Stock Price: IBM trading at $191.5.
    • Buy Call Option: Strike price of $190, expiring in September 2024, costing $6.45 per share.
    • Sell Put Option: Same strike price and expiration, collecting a premium of $5 per share.
    • Net Cost: The net cost to establish the synthetic long position is $1.45 per share.

  5. Outcome and Analysis:

    • Stock Price Increases: If IBM's stock price increases above $190, the synthetic position benefits from the price appreciation.
    • Stock Price Decreases: If the stock price falls below $190, the trader may be obligated to buy the stock, but the net cost basis is lower due to the option premium received.
    • Dividend Capture: Holding the synthetic position over the ex-dividend date effectively captures the dividend.

By understanding and implementing synthetic long positions, traders can enhance their dividend capture strategy, offering the benefits of stock ownership with reduced capital requirements and potentially lower risk. This module provides a comprehensive guide to using synthetic options for dividend capture, combining practical examples with theoretical insights.

lessons.title: Leveraging Call Spread Strategy for Dividend Capture
Short Straddle for Dividend Capture
lessons.content:
A short straddle is an advanced options strategy involving the sale of both a call and a put option at the same strike price and expiration date. This strategy can be used around dividend capture opportunities to potentially profit from minimal price movement while collecting premium from both options.

What is a Short Straddle?

A short straddle is created by:

  • Selling a Call Option: This obligates you to sell the stock at the strike price if the option is exercised.
  • Selling a Put Option: This obligates you to buy the stock at the strike price if the option is exercised.

Both options are sold at the same strike price and expiration date, and you collect premiums from both options.

How It Works for Dividend Capture:

  1. Identify the Ex-Dividend Date: Determine the ex-dividend date of the stock you are interested in. To capture the dividend, you must own the stock before this date.

  2. Set Up the Short Straddle:

    • Sell a Call Option: Choose a call option with a strike price close to the current stock price and an expiration date after the ex-dividend date.
    • Sell a Put Option: Select a put option with the same strike price and expiration date as the call option.

Example Scenario:

Let's say IBM is trading at $191.5, and the ex-dividend date is approaching. You want to capture the dividend and potentially profit from the strategy.

  • Sell Call Option:

    • Sell a call option with a strike price of $191.5, expiring one month after the ex-dividend date.
    • Collect a premium of $6.45 per share, so for one contract (100 shares), you receive $645.

  • Sell Put Option:

    • Sell a put option with the same strike price of $191.5 and the same expiration date.
    • Collect a premium of $5 per share, so for one contract (100 shares), you receive $500.

Net Premium: You collect a total premium of $11.45 per share ($6.45 from the call + $5 from the put), or $1,145 for one contract (100 shares).

Outcome:

  • Minimal Price Movement: If IBM's stock price remains around $191.5, both options expire worthless, and you keep the premiums.
  • Stock Price Increases: If the stock price rises significantly, the call option may be exercised, but the put option expires worthless.
  • Stock Price Decreases: If the stock price falls significantly, the put option may be exercised, but the call option expires worthless.
  • Dividend Capture: By holding the short straddle over the ex-dividend date, you capture the dividend if assigned on the put option.

Conclusion:

A short straddle can be an effective strategy for dividend capture, allowing you to profit from both the premiums collected and the dividend itself. However, it involves significant risk, especially if the stock price moves sharply in either direction. Proper risk management and market analysis are crucial for successfully implementing this strategy.

lessons.title: What will we learn in this chapter?
Summary of the Dividend Capture Strategies with Options Course
lessons.content:
In this course, we've explored various strategies for capturing dividends using options. By integrating options with stock holdings, we've demonstrated how you can enhance your returns, manage risks, and leverage your capital more effectively. Here's a recap of what we've covered:

  1. Introduction to Dividend Capture Strategies: We began by understanding the basics of dividend capture, focusing on the critical dates involved such as the ex-dividend date and the payment date. This foundation is essential for applying any advanced strategies.

  2. Covered Call Strategy: We discussed how selling call options against a long stock position can generate additional income from premiums while still capturing dividends. This strategy works well when you expect the stock price to remain stable or increase slightly.

  3. Protective Put Strategy: We explored how buying put options can protect your stock holdings from significant downside risk while still allowing you to capture dividends. This is especially useful in volatile markets or when holding stocks through uncertain periods.

  4. Synthetic Long Position: We detailed how to create a synthetic long position by buying call options and selling put options at the same strike price. This strategy mimics holding the stock itself but with potentially lower capital requirements and risk.

  5. Diagonal Spread Strategy: We looked at combining stock holdings with a diagonal spread, involving buying and selling options with different expiration dates. This strategy allows for capturing dividends while benefiting from changes in volatility and price movements.

  6. Managing Options Trades: We provided tips and best practices for managing options trades effectively. This includes understanding and monitoring the Greeks, using stop-loss orders, adjusting positions as needed, and staying informed about market conditions.

  7. Real-World Examples and Case Studies: Throughout the course, we used real-world examples, such as IBM, to illustrate how these strategies can be applied in practice. These examples helped solidify the concepts and demonstrate their effectiveness.

By the end of this course, you should have a solid understanding of how to use options to capture dividends and manage your investment portfolio more effectively. Remember to continuously review and practice these strategies to refine your skills and adapt to changing market conditions.

Thank you for participating in the Dividend Capture Strategies with Options course. Happy trading!
